blocks.p: But as for Christian, he was given a reprieve and sent back to prison. He stayed there for a while; but He who overrules all things, holding the power of their rage in his own hand, so arranged it that Christian escaped them for that time and went on his way. And as he went, he sang:

v: your Lord, and you shall be with him
while faithless ones, with all their vain
cry out beneath their dark and hellish
Sing, Faithful, sing, and let your name
for though they killed you, you are still alive!

blocks.p: Now I saw in my dream that Christian did not go on alone. There was a man named Hopeful, made so by watching Christian and Faithful, their words and their conduct in their sufferings at the fair, who joined him and, entering into a covenant of brotherhood, told him he would be his companion. So one man died to bear witness to the truth, and another rose out of his ashes to be Christian’s companion on his pilgrimage. Hopeful also told Christian that there were many more of the men in the fair who would take their time and follow after.
So I saw that soon after they had left the fair, they caught up with a man walking ahead of them, whose name was Self-Interest.
“Where are you from, sir?” they asked him. “And how far are you going this way?”
He told them he came from the town of Fair-speech and was going to the Celestial City, but he did not tell them his name.
“From Fair-speech!” said Christian. “Does anyone good live there?” [Prov. 26:25]
“Yes,” said Self-Interest, “I hope so.”
“Please, sir, what may I call you?” said Christian.
“I am a stranger to you, and you to me. If you’re going this way, I’ll be glad of your company; if not, I must be content.”
“I’ve heard of this town of Fair-speech,” said Christian. “As I remember, they say it’s a wealthy place.”
“Yes, I assure you it is, and I have a great many rich relatives there.”
“Who are your relatives there, if I may be so bold?”

“Almost the whole town. In particular, my Lord Turn-about, my Lord Time-server, and my Lord Fair-speech, from whose ancestors the town first took its name; also Mr. Smooth-man, Mr. Facing-both-ways, and Mr. Anything. And the parson of our parish, Mr. Two-tongues, was my mother’s own brother on her father’s side. To tell you the truth, I’ve become a gentleman of good standing, though my great-grandfather was only a boatman, looking one way and rowing another; and I made most of my fortune in the same line of work.”
“Are you a married man?”

“Yes, and my wife is a very virtuous woman, the daughter of a virtuous woman. She was my Lady Feigning’s daughter, so she comes from a very honorable family, and she has reached such a height of good breeding that she knows how to behave with everyone, prince or peasant. It’s true that we differ somewhat in religion from those of the stricter sort, but only on two small points. First, we never struggle against wind and tide. Second, we are always most zealous when Religion goes about in his silver slippers. We love to walk with him in the street when the sun is shining and the people are applauding him.”

Then Christian stepped a little aside to his companion Hopeful and said, “It occurs to me that this is one Self-Interest of Fair-speech; and if it is, we have as thorough a rogue in our company as lives anywhere in these parts.”
“Ask him,” said Hopeful. “I wouldn’t think he’d be ashamed of his own name.”

So Christian came up to him again and said, “Sir, you talk as if you knew something more than the whole world does; and if I’m not mistaken, I have half a guess who you are. Isn’t your name Mr. Self-Interest, of Fair-speech?”
“That is not my name. It’s a nickname given me by some who can’t stand me, and I must be content to bear it as an insult, as other good men have borne theirs before me.”
“But did you never give people reason to call you by that name?”

“Never, never! The worst I ever did to give them reason was that I always had the luck to make my judgment match the current way of the times, whatever it was, and I happened to profit by it. But if things fall into my lap like that, let me count them a blessing, and let not the spiteful load me with insults for it.”
“I thought you were the man I’d heard of,” said Christian. “And to tell you what I think, I’m afraid that name fits you better than you’d like us to believe.”
“Well, if you choose to think so, I can’t help it. You’ll find me good company, if you’ll still have me with you.”

“If you go with us, you must go against wind and tide, which I see is against your principles. You must also stand by Religion in his rags as well as in his silver slippers, and stand by him when he’s bound in irons as well as when he walks the streets to applause.”
“You must not impose on me or lord it over my faith. Leave me my liberty, and let me go with you.”
“Not a step further, unless you will do as we do in what I’ve said.”

“I will never abandon my old principles,” said Self-Interest, “since they are harmless and profitable. If I may not go with you, I must do as I did before you caught up with me: go by myself, until someone overtakes me who will be glad of my company.”

Now I saw in my dream that Christian and Hopeful left him and kept their distance ahead of him. But one of them, looking back, saw three men following Mr. Self-Interest; and as they came up to him, he made them a very low bow, and they paid him a compliment in return. The men’s names were Mr. Hold-the-world, Mr. Money-love, and Mr. Save-all, men whom Mr. Self-Interest had known before; for in their youth they had been schoolmates, taught by one Mr. Grasp, a schoolmaster in Love-gain, which is a market town in the county of Coveting, in the north. This schoolmaster taught them the art of getting, whether by violence, cheating, flattery, lying, or putting on a show of religion; and these four gentlemen had learned so much of their master’s art that any one of them could have run such a school himself.
Well, when they had greeted each other, as I said, Mr. Money-love said to Mr. Self-Interest, “Who are those on the road ahead of us?” For Christian and Hopeful were still in sight.
“They’re a couple of men from a far country who are going on pilgrimage in their own fashion.”
“Alas! Why didn’t they wait, so that we could have had their good company? For they and we, and you too, sir, I hope, are all going on pilgrimage.”

“We are indeed. But the men ahead of us are so rigid, so in love with their own notions, and think so little of other people’s opinions, that however godly a man may be, if he doesn’t agree with them in everything, they throw him out of their company altogether.”

“That’s bad,” said Mr. Save-all. “But we read of some who are ‘overly righteous,’ and their rigidity leads them to judge and condemn everyone but themselves. But tell me, what were the points you differed on, and how many?”

“Why, in their headstrong way, they conclude that it’s their duty to press on with their journey in all weathers, while I’m for waiting for wind and tide. They are for risking everything for God at one stroke, while I’m for taking every advantage to secure my life and property. They’re for holding to their notions even if everyone else is against them, while I’m for religion in whatever way, and as far as, the times and my safety will allow. They’re for Religion when he’s in rags and contempt, while I’m for him when he walks in golden slippers, in the sunshine, to applause.”

“Yes, and you stick to that, good Mr. Self-Interest,” said Mr. Hold-the-world. “I can only count a man a fool who, being free to keep what he has, is so unwise as to lose it. Let us be as wise as serpents, and make hay while the sun shines. You see how the bee lies still all winter and stirs only when she can have profit with pleasure. God sends rain sometimes, and sometimes sunshine; if they’re fools enough to go through the rain, let us be content to take the fair weather. I like best the religion that goes along with the security of God’s good blessings to us. For what reasonable man could imagine that God, having given us the good things of this life, would not want us to keep them for his sake? Abraham and Solomon grew rich in religion, and Job says a good man will lay up gold like dust. But he must not be like the men ahead of us, if they are as you describe them.”
“I think we’re all agreed on this,” said Mr. Save-all, “so there’s no need for more words about it.”
“No need at all,” said Mr. Money-love. “For a man who believes neither Scripture nor reason, and you see we have both on our side, neither understands his own liberty nor looks after his own safety.”
“My brothers,” said Mr. Self-Interest, “we are all going on pilgrimage, as you see. To keep our minds off bad things, allow me to put a question to you.

“Suppose a man, a minister, or a tradesman, or the like, has an opportunity in front of him to gain the good blessings of this life; but he can’t possibly get them unless, outwardly at least, he becomes extraordinarily zealous on some points of religion he never concerned himself with before. May he use these means to reach his goal, and still be a thoroughly honest man?”

“I see what you’re getting at,” said Mr. Money-love, “and with these gentlemen’s permission I’ll try to answer. First, as your question concerns a minister. Suppose a worthy minister has only a small parish with a poor living, and has his eye on a bigger one, far richer and more comfortable. Suppose he now has the chance to get it, but only by studying harder, preaching more often and more zealously, and, because the mood of the people requires it, changing some of his principles. I see no reason why a man may not do this, provided he has a call, and a great deal more besides, and still be an honest man. Here is why.
“First, his desire for a bigger position is lawful, since Providence has put it in front of him; so he may get it if he can, without troubling his conscience.
“Second, his desire for it makes him more studious and a more zealous preacher, and so a better man. It makes him develop his gifts, which is in keeping with the mind of God.

“Third, as for giving up some of his principles to suit the mood of his people, this shows (1) that he has a self-denying temper; (2) that he has a sweet and winning manner; and so (3) that he is all the more fit to be a minister.

“Fourth, I conclude that a minister who trades a small position for a great one should not be judged greedy. Rather, since his gifts and diligence have improved by it, he should be counted as one who pursues his calling and the opportunity put into his hands to do good.

“Now to the second part, the tradesman. Suppose such a man has only a poor living, but by becoming religious he can improve his business, perhaps marry a rich wife, or get more and better customers. I see no reason why this may not lawfully be done. Here is why.
“First, to become religious is a virtue, by whatever means a man becomes so.
“Second, it is not unlawful to get a rich wife, or more customers for my shop.

“Third, the man who gets these things by becoming religious gets what is good, from those who are good, by becoming good himself. So here is a good wife, good customers, and good profit, all by becoming religious, which is good. Therefore, to become religious in order to get all these is a good and profitable plan.”

Mr. Money-love’s answer to Mr. Self-Interest’s question was highly applauded by them all, and they concluded that it was most sound and advantageous. Because they thought no one could contradict it, and because Christian and Hopeful were still within call, they agreed to confront them with the question as soon as they caught up, all the more because the two had opposed Mr. Self-Interest before. So they called after them, and Christian and Hopeful stopped and waited until they came up. But as they went, the four agreed that old Mr. Hold-the-world, not Mr. Self-Interest, should put the question, because they supposed the pilgrims would answer him without the heat that had flared up between them and Mr. Self-Interest when they parted a little earlier.
So they came up to each other, and after a short greeting, Mr. Hold-the-world put the question to Christian and his companion and told them to answer it if they could.

“Even a newborn in religion could answer ten thousand questions like that,” said Christian. “For if it is wrong to follow Christ for loaves of bread, as it is in the sixth chapter of John, how much more detestable is it to make him and religion a stalking-horse to get and enjoy the world! Nor do we find anyone but heathens, hypocrites, devils, and sorcerers who hold this opinion.

“First, heathens. When Hamor and Shechem wanted Jacob’s daughter and his cattle, and saw that the only way to get them was to be circumcised, they said to their companions, ‘If every male among us is circumcised as they are, won’t their cattle and their goods and all their animals be ours?’ Jacob’s daughter and his cattle were what they were after, and their religion was the stalking-horse they used to get them. Read the whole story. [Gen. 34:20-23]

“Second, the hypocritical Pharisees held this religion too. Long prayers were their pretense, but getting widows’ houses was their intention; and God’s judgment on them was a greater condemnation. [Luke 20:46-47]
“Third, Judas the devil held this religion too. He was religious for the sake of the money bag, so that he could have what was in it. But he was lost, cast away, the very son of perdition.
“Fourth, Simon the sorcerer held this religion too. He wanted the Holy Spirit so that he could make money by it, and the sentence Peter pronounced on him was to match. [Acts 8:19-22]

“Fifth, I can’t get it out of my mind that the man who takes up religion for the sake of the world will throw religion away for the sake of the world. For just as surely as Judas gave up the world in becoming religious, so surely did he sell religion and his Master for it. To answer the question yes, then, as I see you have done, and to accept such an answer as sound, is heathenish, hypocritical, and devilish; and your reward will be according to your works.”

Then they stood staring at one another, but had no answer for Christian. Hopeful also agreed with the soundness of Christian’s answer, so there was a great silence among them. Mr. Self-Interest and his company faltered and hung back, so that Christian and Hopeful could get ahead of them.

Then Christian said to his companion, “If these men cannot stand before the judgment of men, what will they do with the judgment of God? And if they are speechless when dealt with by vessels of clay, what will they do when they are rebuked by the flames of a devouring fire?”
